value.text: Big Apple Pizza restaurant owner Scott Van Duzer has been involved with the Read To Succeed program."With our Read To Succeed, and after three years, we've gotten 40,000 books out there, but I found a way to get books out there a lot quicker," said Van Duzer. It's called the New Worlds Reading program.Amy York, and her son Tripp, read together from books he gets in the mail. "So, he got these books through a program called New Worlds Reading, and they are a partnership with the University of Florida and Scholastic," York said. "Well, it's awesome because they ship the books right to your house."Van Duzer said it's easy getting books. "It takes less than five minutes, and they get nine free books a year through fifth grade." Van Duzer said he wants to help all kids, especially low income children, to have access to books."It's just essential that we get books in kids' hands earlier and to have them in the home," he said, "I think it's just a huge step in their educational journey."Van Duzer feels so strongly about kids improving their reading that he is renovating a part of his restaurant into a reading room. "I believe that it's all children's right to read and having access to books is so important," she said. "One day he can choose whatever career path he wants, but reading is the foundation for all careers."To learn more about New Worlds Reading, click here.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press, keeping the seat in Democratic hands.“I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect,” El-Sayed told supporters in a victory speech late Tuesday."I want you to let them know. Let them know that we, together, fighting for something bigger; we won."El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, made the war in Gaza one of the central issues in his campaign, accusing Israel of committing genocide. support for Israel under President Donald Trump.His background was subject to attack ads from Republicans, who accused him of being part of the Muslim Brotherhood. He shrugged off those attacks and built a coalition of progressive and moderate Democrats that included former President Barack Obama and U.S. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.The final days of the campaign took a dramatic turn when El-Sayed's former Democratic primary opponent, U.S. Haley Stevens, withdrew her endorsement of him and instead backed Rogers. Stevens said she ultimately could not support El-Sayed, citing differences over Israel and saying she did not feel welcome in his campaign.A former public health official, El-Sayed campaigned on expanding access to affordable health care, including his support for Medicare for All.His platform also focused on lowering everyday costs, expanding access to affordable housing, reducing the influence of money in politics and strengthening environmental protections, including efforts to ensure clean air and water.

Democratic challenger Katherine Waldron has defeated incumbent Palm Beach County Commissioner Sara Baxter in the race for the District 6 seat.Baxter, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, lost her bid for another term on the commission to Waldron, a former state lawmaker and Port of Palm Beach commissioner.>> FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election NewsThe race pitted a first-term Republican incumbent against a Democrat with previous experience in elected office.Baxter was elected to the Palm Beach County Commission in 2022, marking her first elected position. She represented District 6, which covers a large portion of western Palm Beach County.Waldron entered the race with experience in both local and state government. She previously served on the Port of Palm Beach District Board of Commissioners and in the Florida House of Representatives.Waldron's victory flips the District 6 seat from Republican to Democratic control and ends Baxter's tenure on the County Commission after one term.

Pete Ricketts will defeat independent challenger Dan Osborn in Nebraska's U.S. Senate race, according to The Associated Press, keeping the seat in Republican hands.Ricketts' victory maintains the GOP's hold on both of Nebraska's U.S. Senate seats, which Republicans have controlled since 2012.RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governorA former Nebraska governor, Ricketts campaigned on strengthening U.S. border security and lowering taxes. He advanced through the Republican primary after defeating four challengers.Ricketts was initially appointed to the Senate in 2023 following the resignation of Republican Ben Sasse. He later won a special election to serve the remainder of Sasse's term.Ricketts' victory preserves Republican control of the seat as the party seeks to maintain its majority in the U.S.

Democrat Brian Poindexter will defeat Republican Rep. Max Miller in Tuesday’s race for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, according to the Associated Press.The race had become one of the more closely watched House contests in the country, shaped by allegations of domestic abuse against Miller made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. Miller has denied the allegations, and the House Ethics Committee has opened an investigation into his conduct.RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governorThe controversy prompted criticism from some prominent Republicans, including Ohio's two U.S. senators, Jon Husted and Bernie Moreno, Emily’s father, who called on Miller to step aside. Miller nevertheless continued his campaign and retained support from President Donald Trump.Poindexter, a union ironworker and former Brook Park city councilman, sought to appeal to working-class voters with a campaign focused on affordability, health care and labor issues. He argued that rising costs and concerns about the economy gave voters reasons to reconsider Republican leadership.Poindexter's victory gives Democrats a pickup in a district that has traditionally leaned Republican.

Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

Democrats will take control of the U.S. House of Representatives after flipping numerous Republican-held seats, according to The Associated Press.The victory, combined with Democrats' takeover of the U.S. Senate, gives the party control of both chambers of Congress.RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governorVotes are still being counted in several House races, leaving the size of Democrats' majority in the next Congress uncertain.Democrats capitalized on voter frustration over affordability, rising gas prices and the war in Iran, issues that dominated the campaign leading up to the midterm elections.House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is positioned to become the next speaker of the House. If elected by his colleagues, Jeffries would make history as the first Black person to hold the position.In a speech Tuesday night, Jeffries spoke about how Democrats would lead. "We understand, as House of Democrats, that we need to deliver dramatic change," he said. We need a Congress that puts the American people first. The wealthy, the well-off, and the well-connected tried to buy this election. The American people have responded in a resounding way and made clear that America is not for sale."The victory marks Democrats' first return to control of the House since January 2023, when Republicans took the majority after four years of Democratic leadership under former Speaker Nancy Pelosi.In the weeks leading up to Election Day, House Speaker Mike Johnson remained confident that Republicans would retain their majority, dismissing polls that suggested Democrats were positioned for a strong showing.President Donald Trump had promised Americans $5,000 payments if Republicans retained control of both the House and Senate, but the incentive was not enough to prevent the party from losing both chambers.

President Donald Trump deflected blame after a slew of Republican losses in Tuesday’s midterm election.“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote on Truth Social.In the month leading up to Election Day, the president held rallies across the country, urging voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on his leadership as Republicans sought to energize his base and boost turnout.Those in Trump’s orbit appeared to shift blame to candidates. A White House official pointed to candidate quality. “President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates themselves,” the official stated.Republican and White House officials believed the president’s rallies helped boost Republican enthusiasm and candidate support in the lead-up to Tuesday, as they focused on turning out low-propensity voters who historically have supported the president."Tonight is further proof that Republican candidates can't take turnout for granted when President Trump isn't on the ballot,” a source with ties to Trump told Scripps News. “President Trump and his operation worked harder than anyone to turn out Republican voters, going above and beyond to make up for some candidates who failed to do the work themselves.”Several Trump-backed candidates lost despite receiving significant attention and support from the president. In Texas, Trump endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton over U.S. John Cornyn in the Republican primary. Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico on Tuesday. In South Carolina, the president backed Sen. Darline Graham, who entered the race following the death of her brother, the late Sen. Graham lost to Democrat Annie Andrews. The mood at the White House shifted from “cautiously optimistic” earlier Tuesday evening to “defiant” as election results came in, according to White House officials. One official said Trump had “left it all out on the field” and “done everything that was needed.”However, other republicans put the onus on Trump.A republican strategist in a competitive race called Tuesday's results a “total and utter rejection of Donald Trump.”“I think much of what we are seeing tonight is a reflection of the Trump agenda, particularly our continued involvement in Iran, high gas prices, inflation and the lack of focus on issues affecting everyday Americans,” said a statewide Republican official.Another republican strategist indicated the results weren’t surprising. “The high tariff and high gas prices had an expiration date,” they said.Some pointed to the president’s top outside political advisers.One strategist said they “…spent this cycle borrowing President Trump’s name and their proximity to him because their own records couldn’t carry the weight. The President built the MAGA movement with his own two hands. They just hitched a ride and good candidates went down with them.”Republicans publicly expressed confidence ahead of Tuesday's elections. Trump also voiced optimism but repeatedly cautioned that the party holding the White House historically struggles in midterm elections.The administration now contends there will be “buyer's remorse.”“Anyone who voted Democrat today is going to have a serious case of buyer's remorse when gas prices come down quickly when the Iran conflict is solved, but they’re still stuck with a list of liberal extremist Democrats,” said a White House official.“Democrats are renting many of these seats, and the independents who voted for them will swing back hard after two years of a socialist majority and a serious case of buyer's remorse,” said a Trump world source.Trump, however, said he would accept the election results, telling The New York Times in an interview, “I am absolutely willing to accept those results.”The results stand to have a significant impact on the president’s remaining time in office.Trump previously indicated to reporters he could rely on veto power in a Democratic-controlled Congress.“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out,” Trump told the New York Times.Earlier in the campaign, a White House official said the legislative affairs team was “probably planning for all scenarios,” though the administration expected a Republican victory.“Regardless of how today plays out, President Trump’s resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger. Buckle up,” a White House official stated.

Angie Nixon’s bid to become Florida's first Black U.S. senator ended in defeat Tuesday, but the Jacksonville Democrat told supporters her fight is far from over."We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over," Nixon said during her concession speech.The Associated Press projected Republican Sen. Ashley Moody the winner of the special election. With votes still being counted, Moody had just over 50% of the vote to Nixon’s approximately 48%.Nixon, a Florida state representative, entered the general election after a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. The progressive candidate campaigned on affordability, championing Medicare for All, free child care and rent freezes.For some supporters, the relatively close race showed an opportunity for Democrats in a state where Republicans have built a substantial advantage.Supporter Mak Manning loved the grassroots campaign Nixon built."She's willing to get out there and into the streets and fight," said Manning.Nixon said Democrats face challenges ahead, including fundraising and closing the voter registration gap with Republicans."That 1.5 million gap in registration, we need to fix that," she told reporters.Asked what comes next, Nixon said her immediate plans included getting some sleep. But she did not rule out another run."I’m looking forward to 2028 because we’re getting to work," she said.

Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

Lucie County School Board Chairman Troy Ingersoll has won a sixth term, defeating political newcomer Lisa Kessler in the District 5 runoff election. District 5 covers the eastern, coastal portion of the school district. Although School Board candidates must live in their districts, all registered St. Lucie County voters were eligible to vote in the nonpartisan race. The August primary was exceptionally close. Kessler received 37.5% of the vote and Ingersoll received 37.2%, a difference of 167 votes; Charles Cerami received 25.2%. AOL Ingersoll has served on the School Board since 2006 and is its current chairman. He owns Pinch A Penny Pools and Spas in Vero Beach and serves as pastor of Midway Road Baptist Church. He holds a criminology degree from Florida State University and a master’s degree from New Orleans Baptist Theological Seminary. theballotbrief.com Ingersoll says his priorities are safe schools, stronger student achievement and responsible budgeting. He supports maintaining accelerated academic programs through consistent funding, targeted interventions and teacher development. He also cites teacher recruitment and retention, managing rapid population growth and developing leadership as major challenges for the district’s next term. AOL Kessler is a small-business owner, bestselling author and chair of the Fort Pierce Arts and Culture Advisory Board. She spent 26 years in sales and marketing management before writing full time. Her campaign also notes that she is the daughter of two lifelong public-school teachers and has served as a Girl Scout troop leader for 11 years. voterfocus.com Kessler’s platform focuses on academic standards in reading, math, science and career readiness; recruiting and retaining qualified teachers; stronger career and technical education; arts programs; and better communication between schools and families. She says public schools should make their case to families by highlighting certified teachers and programs unavailable elsewhere. AOL She also calls for transparent budgeting and treating parents as partners in school decisions. The race asks voters whether to retain Ingersoll’s long board experience and current direction, or choose Kessler’s call for new leadership focused on teacher retention, core academics and family engagement.

Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin in a closely contested race Tuesday, marking a change in leadership for one of Florida's fastest-growing cities. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections , Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Giordano won by 2,601 votes. All 62 precincts have reported, with election-day, early and mail votes marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. Throughout his campaign, he argued that developers should pay their fair share for improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as the city continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion, particularly in St. Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, and Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway. Taxpayer spending was another major issue in the race. Giordano called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall. Martin pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate. The two candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%. Voters reject twice-weekly trash pickup proposal Port St. Lucie voters also overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to pay more for twice-weekly residential trash collection. According to the latest election results, 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The ballot question asked whether residents would support paying an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly garbage collection. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

Rick Meltzer beat Idony Jean Baptist for the open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, which covers the city’s eastern and northeastern areas. The winner succeeds three-term Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, who did not seek reelection. With 58 of 62 precincts reporting, Meltzer won 56.7 percent of the vote to Jean Baptiste's 43.3 percent. Meltzer led the four-candidate August primary with about 42% of the vote, followed by Jean Baptiste at about 22%. Neither reached the majority needed to win outright. Meltzer is a mortgage loan originator, has lived in District 1 for more than 20 years and has coached and mentored youth sports for 17 years. He is a political newcomer who says he would bring an outsider’s perspective to City Hall. His platform focuses on affordability, accountability and infrastructure. Meltzer says he would seek budget cuts and lower property taxes, hold contractors and developers to project deadlines and budgets, and prioritize road, utility and other infrastructure needs before approving new development. He also opposes more zero-lot-line housing and supports building a sports complex. Full local election results Meltzer has also said he is researching the impacts of data centers, including water use, electricity demand and noise. He says their potential tax revenue and jobs could outweigh the concerns if the city protects residents’ interests. Jean Baptiste is a minister and former Indian River County Sheriff’s Office detention deputy. He previously ran for the same seat in 2022 and later briefly filed to run for St. Lucie County sheriff before withdrawing. His campaign emphasizes safer communities, transparent government, listening to residents, helping people in need and supporting small businesses. Jean Baptiste has proposed attracting more businesses to grow city revenue and reduce service costs for residents, along with moving to a double-can automated trash-pickup system that he says could improve service and save money. The choice is between Meltzer’s call for tighter spending oversight and infrastructure-first growth, and Jean Baptiste’s focus on community responsiveness, public safety and service improvements.

Democrat Troy Jackson defeated Republican U.S. Susan Collins in Maine on Tuesday, flipping a Republican-held seat and expanding the Democrats' newly secured Senate majority.RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governorA spokesperson for Troy Jackson said Collins called to concede the Senate race. Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, got into the race after Graham Platner withdrew following allegations of sexual assault, which he denied. "A little more than a hundred days ago, I stood in front of our convention and asked you to put your faith in a logger from Allagash," Jackson told a crowd of supporters. "You know, I told you that, you know, we had a party to unite, a movement to build, and a senator to defeat. Well, tonight, again this morning, the people of Maine have elected that logger to the United States Senate."Jackson campaigned on affordability, health care and workers' rights while criticizing policies supported by President Donald Trump. He argued that Collins had become too closely aligned with the Trump administration, particularly on issues affecting working families.Collins, who was seeking a sixth term, built a reputation as a moderate Republican and emphasized her seniority, experience and ability to secure federal funding for Maine. She highlighted her work on the Senate Appropriations Committee, arguing that her relationships in Washington helped deliver critical resources to the state.

Florida voters have approved Amendment 3, a sweeping constitutional amendment that will change the state's property tax system by increasing the homestead exemption, reducing assessment increases on non-homestead properties and restricting how counties and municipalities can use property tax revenue.WATCH REPORT BELOW: >> FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election NewsWith 99% of precincts reporting at 10:13 p.m., 62% voted Yes while 38% voted No.Amendment 3 required support from at least 60% of voters to become part of the Florida Constitution. Under the amendment, the homestead exemption for property taxes other than school district taxes will increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beginning in 2029, the exemption will be adjusted for inflation. The amendment also establishes different rules for newer Florida residents. New residents will receive a smaller exemption until they have lived in the state for five years. Amendment 3 also changes how quickly the assessed value of non-homestead properties, including rental and commercial properties, can rise. The annual assessment cap will decrease from 10% to 5%, except for school district taxes. Another provision restricts how counties and municipalities can spend property tax revenue, directing that revenue toward specified purposes including public safety, education, infrastructure, natural resource and flood-control projects, local bonds, employee retirement benefits and government operations. The proposal was placed on the ballot by the Florida Legislature during a special session in June. The changes will take effect Jan.

Families in Riviera Beach's Lone Pine Estates community are dealing with floodwater inside their homes, power outages and dwindling supplies after about 15.5 inches of rain inundated the city, prompting evacuations and straining the city's wastewater system. Crews were using pumps and vacuum trucks Tuesday to remove water while fire rescue teams used rafts to help residents navigate flooded streets. Ron DeSantis to add Palm Beach County to the state emergency declaration, which could help open the door to federal FEMA assistance.For Susana Perez, seeing water reach her home was overwhelming."I was really sad. I started to cry," Perez told WPTV. "I never saw something like that before in all these years I've lived here."Riviera Beach police Maj. Myers said the city received about 15.5 inches of rain and crews were deploying resources in an effort to reduce the amount of standing water.The flooding is also putting pressure on Riviera Beach's wastewater infrastructure. City officials said a wastewater force main ruptured across Blue Heron Boulevard, adding to infrastructure problems caused by the flooding.Richard Gallant, the city's assistant utility director, urged residents to reduce their water use."Try not to flush your toilets. Try not to use any excessive water," Gallant said.WPTV cameras captured fire rescue crews using rafts to move through flooded streets and help residents.Perez, a Lone Pine Estates resident whose family was helped out by fire rescue, thanked crews for assisting the neighborhood."They were helping everybody in the neighborhood," Perez said. "God bless them, and we really do appreciate them for sure."The city said emergency teams would stop entering flooded communities for routine assistance after 6 p.m. Tuesday, with crews continuing to respond to medical emergencies and life-threatening situations. Officials urged anyone needing evacuation assistance to contact the Emergency Operations Center before the cutoff. Residents seeking nonemergency assistance can contact the city's Emergency Operations Center at 877-257-2374, according to WPTV's continuing coverage. For families still surrounded by water, the next question is how quickly conditions will improve.Lawson cautioned that the damage will not disappear when the floodwaters recede."This is not an overnight recovery," he said.City officials are coordinating bottled water and ready-to-eat meals for affected families, while crews continue working to restore safe conditions. For Lone Pine Estates residents, that recovery begins with getting the water out of their neighborhood and assessing what remains once it is gone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Steven Giordano has won the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, defeating incumbent Shannon Martin after a closely watched campaign.Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. He defeated Martin by a margin of just over 2,400 votes.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The outcome marked a significant turnaround from the August primary, when Martin finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of Giordano.Speaking at his election-night watch party, Giordano said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race."I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons," Giordano said. "I think they watched the debate."Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician."I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people," he said. Surrounded by Democratic constituents and fellow Democratic winners celebrating at an election night watch party in West Palm Beach, Lois Frankel was already looking beyond her victory Tuesday night.The Democratic congresswoman won Florida's newly redrawn 23rd Congressional District, defeating Republican Deborah Adeimy and securing an eighth term in Congress. Democrat Pia Dandiya has won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, defeating Republican Casey Askar in Tuesday's general election and keeping a closely watched congressional seat in Democratic hands.Dandiya's victory comes after a dramatic redrawing of the district, which once reliably favored Democrats but now includes Republican strongholds across Palm Beach, Broward, Collier and Hendry counties.WATCH BELOW: Pia Dandiya says she'll stand up to 'corruption' in D.C.The new boundaries created uncertainty over which party would win the seat — and made the race significant far beyond South Florida.District 22 was one of four Florida congressional districts redrawn in ways that could help Republicans flip Democratic seats and strengthen their position in Congress. Dandiya's victory denies Republicans one potential pickup in their fight for control of the U.S. House.Supporters erupted in cheers Tuesday night at the Wellington Community Center as Dandiya took the stage to celebrate her victory.The Florida-born former teacher and high school principal thanked voters and pledged to deliver on the promises that shaped her campaign, including lowering the cost of living and tackling what she describes as corruption in Washington."My commitment to you is that I will work tirelessly to lower the cost of living, to stand up to the corruption in DC, so you can spend less time worrying about how you will make ends meet and more time building the life for your family that you want," Dandiya told supporters.Throughout her campaign, Dandiya made affordability a central issue, promising to make the American Dream more attainable for South Florida families.In a previous interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Dandiya outlined several proposals aimed at easing financial pressures and protecting federal benefits.Those included expanding Affordable Care Act subsidies, allowing Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices and potentially raising the Social Security payroll tax cap to help preserve benefits.She also pledged to work across party lines to address issues facing families throughout the newly drawn district."I'm not going to Washington to fight with people. I'm going to fight for people," Dandiya said in a statement released Tuesday night.The 22nd Congressional District underwent significant changes ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.Previously represented by Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel, the district was redrawn to stretch across South Florida, connecting coastal and inland communities with different political backgrounds.Frankel instead sought reelection in the newly drawn 23rd Congressional District.The changes set up a competitive race between Dandiya and Askar, with Republicans hoping the new boundaries would give them an opportunity to flip the seat.In her victory statement, Dandiya reflected on her family's journey to the United States and what her election means to her personally."More than 40 years ago, my parents came from India to Palm Beach County, determined to live the American Dream," Dandiya said. "And tonight, one generation later, their daughter will become Congresswoman Dandiya."Dandiya, who was born and raised in Palm Beach County, previously worked at Apple and served as a White House Fellow, in addition to her experience in education.She also pledged to work across party lines to address issues facing South Florida families."Whether you are from Belle Glade or Marco Island, Parkland or Royal Palm, I will work tirelessly to lower the cost of living and stand up to the corruption in DC," she said.Dandiya will serve a two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives."Thank you for trusting me with a part in its next chapter," Dandiya said. "Let's make it one our children will be proud to read."

Brian Mast has won another term in Congress, defeating Democratic challenger James Martin in Florida's 21st Congressional District.Mast, a U.S. Army veteran who has served in Congress since 2017, secured reelection in the newly redrawn district, which includes portions of Palm Beach, Martin and St. Lucie counties.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Brian Mast wins reelection >> FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News Mast said one of his biggest priorities is to continue the battle for clean water."They think they're going to go into next summer on a high Lake (Okeechobee) instead of a low lake, so they're already thinking about where, when, how much water they’re going to put in different places; that is a day-to-day fight. Byron Donalds was elected Florida's first Black governor on Tuesday in a race that was seen as unexpectedly competitive down the stretch, defeating Democratic nominee David Jolly.Donalds will succeed outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who used the office to fan presidential ambitions and steer President Donald Trump's adopted home state further to the right.WATCH REPORT BELOW:>> FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News The race presented a test of whether Trump's unpopularity, which has dragged down Republicans across the U.S., would extend to his backyard and endanger an office in Florida that a Democrat hasn't won in more than 30 years.Jolly is a former Republican congressman who switched parties and ran a centrist campaign. Donalds had sought to define him as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats.WATCH BELOW: Byron Donalds' victory speechBeyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes.Florida spent a generation as America's prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point.That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender — signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as "Don't Say Gay" that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state's Democrats in shambles.Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party's rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising.Seeking to overcome those challenges, Jolly campaigned in Florida's Democratic strongholds, like Broward County, along with traditionally Republican parts of central Florida and the state's Panhandle.Donalds maintained a steady confidence throughout the campaign, balancing his support for Trump with efforts to create some distance, including minimizing references to the president on his website.

Jared Moskowitz has won reelection in Florida’s 25th Congressional District, defeating Republican challenger and former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer.Moskowitz thanked voters Tuesday night for sending him back to Washington, saying economic concerns were central to his campaign.WATCH REPORT BELOW: >> FULL ELECTION RESULTS | Latest Election News "Very thankful to the voters of District 25 for giving me another opportunity to send me to Washington," Moskowitz said. "This race was about affordability. We listened to people in the district. We didn't excuse it as a hoax," Moskowitz said. "People are struggling."Moskowitz also pointed to the amount of money spent in the closely watched congressional race, arguing that Republican efforts to defeat him ultimately failed."They wasted $26 million trying to take me out, on a seat that they gerrymandered that I shouldn't have been able to win," Moskowitz said. "This was the most expensive congressional seat in Florida history, and they lit their money on fire, and the voters sent them a message."The $26 million figure and Moskowitz's characterization of the district and race spending were claims he made in his election-night remarks.Moskowitz released the following statement after winning reelection:"Tonight, South Florida sent a clear message: voters want leaders who think for themselves, stand up to extremes, and deliver results. This district was re-drawn to defeat me. I am deeply grateful to everyone who placed their trust in me, and to the volunteers and supporters who made this victory possible. Whether you voted for me or not, I will work every day to earn your trust and represent every corner of this district."Throughout this campaign, I never changed who I am or what I believe. I stood up to the extremes on the left that targeted me in the primary and to the extremes on the right that spent more money against me than anyone in Florida history." "As I return to Washington, fighting to lower the cost of living will be a top priority. The cost of groceries, gas, and home insurance is putting too much pressure on South Florida families and they need relief. I will work with anyone to achieve progress for my constituents as I have done throughout my public service."I will also continue confronting antisemitism and hate, whether it comes from the far right or the far left. My grandmother escaped Berlin through the Kindertransport. My family’s story is a constant reminder that standing up to hate requires courage and action. I will never be silent, and I will never let party politics determine when I speak out."The campaign might be over, but the work continues. I am ready to get back to Washington to continue representing residents of South Florida."

Lucie County officials said Tuesday that emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls as they responded to widespread flooding after historic rainfall. Lucie County Fire District received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period, Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said at a county briefing. The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. Guerrero said the county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Officials were continuing high-water rescues, assessing roads and infrastructure, and working with public works crews to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns, he said. Please use caution and avoid unnecessary travel, Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said. It may take several days for the water to recede. Shelters open; schools closed Wednesday The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, and the county landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. He said the district had not seen significant water intrusion in its schools but would assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Lucie officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. The city said vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000 . The city also warned residents to expect a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday. Officials urge residents to avoid floodwater Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and neighborhoods that had been evacuated. He warned against taking advantage of residents affected by flooding and said the Sheriff’s Office would take those cases seriously. See also: LIST: Flooded St. Lucie, Indian River roads remain hazardous as crews check homes Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Guerrero said emergency dispatchers had received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Officials said call takers were screening requests so emergency vehicles could remain available for urgent situations. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

Election Day is here, and voters in Port St. Lucie are heading to the polls Tuesday to decide who will lead one of Florida’s fastest-growing cities for the next four years. Incumbent Mayor Shannon Marti n is facing challenger Steven Giordano in a runoff election after neither candidate secured a majority of the vote in August. The race comes as residents continue to raise concerns about rapid growth, traffic congestion, infrastructure improvements, development and taxpayer spending. Meanwhile, widespread flooding across St. Lucie County has forced election officials to temporarily relocate several polling places ahead of Tuesday’s vote. Where the mayoral race stands Martin finished first in the August primary with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22%. Eric Strazzeri, who finished third with 17.07%, was eliminated from the race. That leaves approximately 6,700 voters who supported Strazzeri in August potentially playing a key role in deciding the outcome of Tuesday’s election. Both candidates have spent the months leading up to Election Day making their case to residents about the future of Port St. Martin is campaigning on her record, pointing to infrastructure improvements and roadwork already underway. Giordano, a longtime Port St. Lucie resident, business owner and former deputy, has called for slowing development until infrastructure can catch up with the city’s rapid growth. He has also called for a new traffic study. The candidates have different visions for how the city should use its land and approach future development. We already have 50 something parks here in Port St Lucie, we didn’t need another 23 acre park or 26 acre park in Tradition, lets utilize that space better, Giordano told CBS12 News. Martin has defended the city’s investments in parks and recreational spaces, saying they reflect what residents have requested. We have developed amazing parks in this city, our residents have asked for that and we have delivered on that and really its about what our residents tell us that they want, Martin said. The two also differ on plans involving a proposed soccer stadium and efforts to create a downtown destination with restaurants, shopping and entertainment. The winner will help shape the city’s future as Port St. Lucie continues to experience significant population growth. Trash collection also on the ballot Beyond the mayoral race, Port St. Lucie voters will also weigh in on another issue that has generated debate across the city: trash collection . Residents are being asked whether they support increasing residential trash pickup from once a week to twice a week at an additional cost. The proposal would increase the city’s annual solid waste assessment by at least $131 beginning in 2028, with additional increases expected in subsequent years. The additional pickup would apply to household garbage, not recycling, yard waste or bulk collection. The ballot question is nonbinding, meaning the results will help city leaders gauge public opinion, but the City Council will ultimately decide whether to move forward with the change. For the latest updates, voters can visit www.stlucievotes.gov or contact the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500. State of emergency declared amid widespread flooding The polling location changes come after days of heavy rainfall left roadways flooded and impassable across parts of St. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways. Lucie police have also extended shifts for officers to provide additional assistance as crews monitor flooding and respond to calls for service. According to the city, several major roadways were closed as of Monday evening, including the intersection of California and Savona boulevards and Port St. Lucie Boulevard at Aviation Avenue. Voters should confirm their assigned precinct, especially if their normal polling location has been affected by flooding. Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

The Treasure Coast is under a local state of emergency after heavy rains caused severe flooding, leaving neighborhoods submerged, roads impassable and residents struggling to navigate the area. On Del Rio Boulevard in Port St. Lucie, drivers are being forced to find alternative routes. “This is crazy, the amount of rain we’ve had in the last few weeks, and now the ground is so saturated,” Ryan Murray, a resident, said. Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students one hour early Monday and cancel all after-school activities as heavy rainfall and flooding continue to impact the county. The district announced that all students will be dismissed one hour earlier than their regularly scheduled dismissal times. All after-school activities, including aftercare programs, have also been canceled. The changes come after parts of St. Lucie County received up to 6 inches of rain. Heavy rain is flooding roadways across the Treasure Coast, leaving drivers stranded, disrupting daily routines and prompting police to urge residents to stay off the roads unless travel is absolutely necessary.WATCH OUR COVERAGE HERE: Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie, floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas, turning roadways into lakes and covering sidewalks. Vehicles that attempted to drive through the water stalled, leaving drivers waiting for help as passing cars sent waves toward already stranded vehicles.Port St. Lucie police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters.One driver told WPTV his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children."I'm on hold with the insurance company right now trying to get some help," he said.The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have gotten worse following heavy rain events.Another woman found herself stranded after her vehicle stopped working just minutes after driving toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard."Every time a car comes by, it pushes my car," she told WPTV.The woman could only speak to WPTV through a small opening in her driver's side door as water continued to rush toward her vehicle. A nearby man eventually tried to help her get out.A couple nearby also described watching their vehicle sink deeper into the floodwaters after being stranded for about an hour, with waves from passing traffic pushing the car around.WATCH BELOW: Aerial video of flooding in St. Lucie WestFor some residents, the flooding created more than just a driving hazard. It also raised concerns about getting children to and from school.One woman told WPTV she was trying to figure out how to pick up her children after parents were notified they needed to retrieve their students."They just announced it, they just called parents right now to pick up kids from school. They let the kids go to school knowing it was like this," she said.She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road just last year."It was only three months old, and she got stuck here on the road because the drainage system here sucks, is so bad," she said.The woman questioned whether the city's road expansion efforts are being matched with improvements to its drainage infrastructure."They just keep widening the roads, not even worried about anything else," she said.The city says it is working on longer-term drainage improvements, including a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood.Plans include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding.However, the project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and working to clear debris from drainage systems.Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.Port St. Lucie police are asking residents to stay home and avoid traveling unless absolutely necessary.Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and remind drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

Steven Giordano has won the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, defeating incumbent Shannon Martin after a closely watched campaign.Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. He defeated Martin by a margin of just over 2,400 votes.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The outcome marked a significant turnaround from the August primary, when Martin finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of Giordano.Speaking at his election-night watch party, Giordano said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race."I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons," Giordano said. "I think they watched the debate."Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician."I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people," he said. "And I'm proud to be the people's mayor."The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave, according to the reporter's script.WPTV reached out to Martin for comment following the election results but had not received a response as of Tuesday night.Read more of WPTV's related coverage below:

Several neighborhoods in Vero Beach were flooded Monday after rounds of heavy rain moved through the area. The scene along 41st Avenue and 12th Street, about a mile from Glendale Elementary School, showed water covering roads, front lawns and driveways. Neighbors said they have never seen flooding this severe in the area before. Residents say the steady rain throughout the day overwhelmed drainage systems, leaving water with nowhere to go but into neighborhood streets and yards. A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed just how high the water rose at one point, with only the roof of an SUV visible above the floodwaters. Authorities have not said whether anyone was inside the vehicle. See also: See updated polling locations due to severe weather across South Florida Deputies are urging residents to stay off the roads and avoid driving through flooded areas, warning that conditions remain unsafe. A CBS12 News crew will be back in affected neighborhoods Tuesday morning to assess any damage as residents continue waiting for floodwaters to recede.

Indian River County Utilities is monitoring conditions and has contacted affected customers. The sheriff's office said if residents had questions or wanted to report their status, they should call 772-226-4000. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin as Port St. Lucie mayor by 2,601 votes
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail voting results were marked complete as of 12:34 a.m.

Throughout the campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share for infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion. On city spending, Giordano called for an independent forensic audit and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. On taxpayer spending, Martin cited 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The nonbinding referendum provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.
hero.article_text: Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin in a closely contested race Tuesday, marking a change in leadership for one of Florida's fastest-growing cities. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections , Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Giordano won by 2,601 votes. All 62 precincts have reported, with election-day, early and mail votes marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. Throughout his campaign, he argued that developers should pay their fair share for improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as the city continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion, particularly in St. Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard and Savona Boulevard, and Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway. Taxpayer spending was another major issue in the race. Giordano called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall. Martin pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate. The two candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%. Voters reject twice-weekly trash pickup proposal Port St. Lucie voters also overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to pay more for twice-weekly residential trash collection. According to the latest election results, 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The ballot question asked whether residents would support paying an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly garbage collection. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County schools closed Wednesday as flood recovery could take seven days
cards.teaser: The county opened a shelter at Northport K-8 School as crews responded to flooding. Officials urged residents to stay home if possible and reserve 911 for life-threatening emergencies.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County schools are closed Wednesday after flooding disrupted road access and left students walking through standing water to get home Monday. County leaders warned that conditions could take up to seven days to return to normal as emergency crews continued their flood response.

Superintendent Jon Prince said the district expects to reopen schools Thursday if roads are clear. During a Tuesday news conference, he apologized to families for the stress caused by Monday’s conditions and said the district had not anticipated the extent of the flooding.

The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals and coffee. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials asked residents to stay home if they can and call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.

In the Tradition area, a private security company that patrols homeowners associations joined rescue efforts with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. Matchton said the crews set out to help people wherever they could with the resources they had.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods. He warned that anyone who preys on flood victims would face zero tolerance. Del Toro emphasized that responders were working together to serve the community.

Flooding also forced Election Day polling-place changes. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to voting sites. The changes included moving voting from Oak Hammock K-8 School and the Disabled American Veterans Hall to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, and from the Paula A. Lewis Library and The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall.
cards.article_text: Lucie County election officials to move six precincts’ polling places on Election Day, including several in Port St. The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves are meant to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Lucie, voters in precincts 49 and 71, who normally cast ballots at Oak Hammock K-8 School, will vote at the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, will also go to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard. Voters in precincts 67 and 86 will not vote at Centennial High School in St. They will vote at Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence, at 500 NW California Blvd. The county says access is from Peacock Boulevard. See also: Inside David Jolly's election night watch party as Florida chooses its next governor In the Tradition area, precinct 83 voters will move from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters will also move from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall. In Fort Pierce, Precinct 12 voters will move from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1. The notice does not list any polling places as closed. It also does not say whether voters who already went to their normal location will be redirected on site. The flooding also disrupted schools. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince apologized to families during a news conference Tuesday, after students were seen walking through standing water to get home Monday. We didn’t anticipate anything like what transpired yesterday. Caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry, Prince said. Schools are closed Wednesday. Prince said the district expects to reopen Thursday if roads are clear, and that no school buildings took significant water. A private security company that patrols homeowners associations in the Tradition area joined the rescue effort with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. We had no goal when we came out here. We had just ambition to figure out how we can help anyone and anywhere and do whatever we can with the resources that we have, Matchton said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods, and warned that anyone who preys on flood victims will face zero tolerance. The sheriff said there was no playbook for a storm like this. But the most important thing is we’re all working together with one purpose, which is to serve this community, Del Toro said. The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

cards.headline: Fort Pierce restaurant owner promotes free books, renovates space for reading room
cards.teaser: Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is helping children get books mailed to their homes through New Worlds Reading while turning part of his restaurant into a reading room.
cards.body:
FORT PIERCE, Fla. Scott Van Duzer, owner of Big Apple Pizza, is working to connect children with free books mailed to their homes while renovating part of his restaurant into a reading room. He wants to expand access to books for children, especially those from low-income families.

Van Duzer has been involved with Read To Succeed, which he said has distributed 40,000 books over three years. He is now promoting New Worlds Reading as a way to get books to children more quickly. Van Duzer said signing up takes less than five minutes and children receive nine free books a year through fifth grade.

Amy York and her son Tripp read together using books he receives through New Worlds Reading. York described the program as a partnership with the University of Florida and Scholastic. “Well, it's awesome because they ship the books right to your house,” York said.

The reading room renovation is another part of Van Duzer’s effort to help children improve their reading. He emphasized the importance of giving children access to books early and keeping books in their homes. “It's just essential that we get books in kids' hands earlier and to have them in the home,” he said.

hero.headline: Angie Nixon concedes Florida U.S. Senate special election to Ashley Moody
hero.body:
Democrat Angie Nixon conceded Florida’s U.S. Senate special election Tuesday after Republican Sen. Ashley Moody was projected to win, with votes still being counted.

Moody had just over 50% of the vote to Nixon’s approximately 48% as counting continued. Nixon, a Jacksonville Democrat and Florida state representative, had sought to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator.

In her concession speech, Nixon told supporters she would continue fighting for her progressive agenda. “We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over,” she said.

Nixon entered the general election after a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. Her campaign focused on affordability, with proposals including Medicare for All, free child care and rent freezes. Some supporters viewed the relatively close race as an opportunity for Democrats in a state where Republicans have built a substantial advantage.

Supporter Mak Manning praised Nixon’s grassroots campaign. “She's willing to get out there and into the streets and fight,” Manning said.

Nixon identified fundraising and closing the voter registration gap with Republicans as challenges facing Democrats. “That 1.5 million gap in registration, we need to fix that,” she said.

Asked about her next steps, Nixon said her immediate plans included getting some sleep. She also looked toward another election cycle: “I’m looking forward to 2028 because we’re getting to work,” she said.
